papers.title: Deterministic Network Interface Naming on Multi-NIC Linux Systems: A Boot-Time Convergence Approach
papers.summary: Network interface naming on multi-NIC Linux systems suffers from a well-documented race condition in systemd-udevd that has remained unsolved since 2017. When multiple network interfaces are present, parallel udev worker threads attempt to rename interfaces simultaneously, causing EEXIST failures when a target name is temporarily occupied by another interface awaiting its own rename. The upstream systemd project has classified this as "not-a-bug" and declines to implement a fix. The problem, previously cosmetic under NetworkManager, has become critical as the industry migrates to systemd-networkd, which matches interfaces by name rather than MAC address, turning a failed rename into a complete loss of network connectivity. This paper presents a boot-time convergence approach that combines systemd .link file declarations with a retry-based init service that detects and recovers from rename failures before dependent services start. Deployed across diverse multi-NIC hardware configurations, the solution achieves 100% deterministic interface naming. The approach is OS-agnostic and applicable to any systemd-based Linux distribution.

papers.title: Streaming OS Installation from Compressed Partitioned Images on Memory-Constrained Bare-Metal Hosts
papers.summary: Bare-metal server provisioning systems typically decompress OS images into RAM before writing them to disk. When servers have insufficient RAM to hold the decompressed image (increasingly common as OS images grow due to AI/ML toolkits, GPU drivers, and firmware stacks), provisioning fails entirely. This paper presents a streaming installation technique that combines partial decompression for metadata extraction with pipeline-based disk writing, enabling OS installation on hosts where available RAM is less than the decompressed image size. The method decompresses only the first 30MB of a compressed image to extract the GPT partition table, calculates the target filesystem offset, then streams the full image through a kernel pipe buffer (64KB) directly to disk at the calculated offset, never storing the decompressed data in memory or on disk. Deployed across a production fleet of memory-constrained bare-metal servers, the technique achieves 100% provisioning success where the standard approach fails entirely.

papers.title: HippocamPEX: A Hippocampus-Inspired In-Silico Architecture for Context-Aware Sequence Prediction
papers.summary: The brain's hippocampus enables episodic memory - the ability to encode events within their context, organize them into sequences, and generate predictive representations to guide adaptive behavior. Modern computing architectures, however, are optimized for large-scale arithmetic and struggle with such context-dependent sequential prediction or "cognitive" tasks. To translate these capabilities into a mixed-signal architecture, we first derived a working model from the neuroscience literature distilling key hippocampal computations into engineering-friendly abstractions. We then leveraged converging advances in in-memory computing, neuromorphic computing, asynchronous circuits, and analog computing to design a mixed-signal hardware architecture implementing these computations, called HippocamPEX. Finally, we demonstrated that HippocamPEX reproduces characteristic representational dynamics of hippocampal subregions and performs robust context-specific sequence prediction through detailed activity and circuit simulations. By tightly coupling hardware design with neuroscience knowledge, this work establishes a pathway for artificial systems capable of rapid, adaptive, and context-aware decision-making, addressing a central gap between biological and conventional computing.

papers.title: Unlocking Turing Tensor Cores: A Measured Throughput Account of From-Scratch Pre-training on a Single 22G RTX 2080 Ti
papers.summary: The RTX 2080 Ti (TU102) ships full second-generation Tensor Cores in hardware, yet the vendor throttles FP16 matrix multiplication at the driver level, leaving usable tensor throughput well below the hardware peak. turing-unlock lifts this restriction with a kernel module that, before the nvidia driver binds the device, writes the FP16 speed selectors (SS0=0x88888888, SS1=0x8) and releases the ACR mutex; published measurements report cuBLAS FP16 matmul throughput rising from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS (about 1.6x). On the same 22G 2080 Ti and under the same from-scratch pre-training protocol as the companion memory ledger (five tiers of Chinese encoder-decoder models, 2,451 steps per tier, 16,384 tokens per step, seed 42), we obtain a before/after throughput account: the small tier (75.7M parameters, 512-wide, 8+8 layers, activation checkpointing on) improves in steady-state throughput from 6,480 to 7,246 tok/s (+11.8%) with wall time cut from 1.77h to 1.61h (9.0% saved); the tiny tier goes from 15,150 to 15,866 tok/s (+4.7%) with wall time savings of 3.8%; the three smaller tiers (pico-micro) gain at most +0.3%; per-tier peak memory stays bit-identical, and final quality metrics are bit-identical or consistent within 10^-3. We conclude that the unlock gain is a function of matrix size, rising monotonically with tier -- imperceptible for pico-micro, visible from tiny upward, and cashed out as a double-digit percentage at small -- and that it is a pure throughput gain that leaves training dynamics untouched.

papers.title: Energy-efficient End-to-End Communication System with Spiking Neural Networks
papers.summary: 2030 is expected to witness the first commercial 6G systems. However, traditional modular communication architectures cannot meet the latency, optimisation, and integration requirements demanded by various sub-millisecond, data-intensive emerging 6G applications. End-to-end (E2E) communication addresses these limitations by replacing traditional processing blocks with neural networks. Nevertheless, conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs) in E2E systems use dense computation. This results in substantial energy consumption and computational resource requirements, which may not be feasible in resource constrained devices. This paper addresses the aforementioned challenge by developing a spiking neural network (SNN) encoder that targets lower encoder inference energy while maintaining communication reliability. In particular, the SNN encoder combines sparse spike activity, sinusoidal temporal modulation, and weighted temporal aggregation to map one-hot encoded messages to distinguishable transmit signals. The model is evaluated across antenna configurations and SNN timesteps to investigate the bit error rate (BER)-energy trade-off. The simulation results show that the SNN encoder achieves comparable BER under suitable timestep selections, while reducing the average estimated encoder energy by 68.93%, 52.20%, and 35.69% for SNN timesteps 2, 3, and 4, respectively, across five antenna configurations. These findings highlight the potential of the proposed SNN encoder for energy-efficient E2E communication systems.

papers.title: Runway Characters: Serving a 57B Video Diffusion Transformer for Real-Time Conversation
papers.summary: Conversational video characters must generate video as fast as it plays, for one user at a time: at 24 fps, a sustained 166.7 ms per four-frame chunk at batch size one, with only a few chunks of buffering. We describe the system behind Runway Characters, which serves a $\approx$57B-parameter autoregressive video diffusion transformer (four denoising passes per chunk) at 704$\times$1088 and 24 fps on four H100 GPUs with a voice agent in the loop. Each chunk takes 240 attention calls, each reading a 5,788-slot KV cache in which only 757 tokens are new, and 29% of the original step was whole-cache work repeated in every call. We move that work to write time (a ring cache, RoPE and FP8 quantization applied once per write, and a delta rotation when positions reset), fuse the tensor-parallel all-reduce into the FP8 GEMM with in-switch reduction, and give the decoder that turns latents into video frames its own GPU. Without the fused kernel, our optimizations cut the diffusion step from 240.9 to 159.3 ms (1.51$\times$, 24.5 fps sustained) with no detected degradation in lip-sync scores; the fused kernel, rolled back once in production and since re-enabled, reaches 147.4 ms (1.63$\times$, 43% of FP8 peak). In seven weeks of production the worker averaged above 23.5 fps in 99.5% of sessions that streamed for at least a second, and our pipeline takes 0.49 s of a 2.1 s median conversational turn. On the same GPUs, the two open-source real-time video systems we benchmarked, at four denoising passes, miss real time or add over a second of latency (one by estimate), at a third to half of our resolution.

papers.title: Demystifying Information Flow Downgrading using the Real--Ideal Paradigm
papers.summary: The real--ideal paradigm, an approach to security specification developed in the cryptography community, has the benefit that it can express sophisticated confidentiality and integrity requirements, even for decentralized systems. We show that this paradigm is the basis for a powerful and intuitive new semantic framework for language-based security. Our new framework cleanly and extensionally captures existing security definitions, including not only noninterference but also less understood information flow properties that involve downgrading, such as robust declassification and nonmalleable information flow. Past semantics for these properties have relied on intensional downgrading events. Further, we show that all of these properties can be enforced by a practical information-flow type system for a while-language that supports downgrading. Surprisingly, correctness of this type system is also characterized as a real--ideal simulation, with an important implication: the security of heterogeneous, decentralized systems with a strong (real) attacker can be understood by reasoning about a weak (ideal) attacker whose power is restricted to interaction with downgrading. This result explains the usefulness of nonmalleable information flow and related security properties. The results are fully formalized using the Rocq prover and are publicly available.

papers.title: Energy-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for language models alternates between generating responses and training the policy. These stages place different demands on GPUs, creating opportunities to reduce clock frequency with little loss in throughput. Selecting frequencies online is difficult because response lengths change and frequency trials themselves consume time and energy. We present EE-RL (energy-efficient RL), an online controller that selects separate frequencies for generation and training during RL execution. It compares candidate settings with a prediction of the default GPU governor on the same token workload, and keeps the most energy-efficient setting that meets a throughput threshold. The controller then monitors throughput and energy and adjusts frequencies as the workload changes. Fixed-frequency sweeps on H100 and GB200 show GPU energy savings of up to 28.2% per valid training token across synchronous and asynchronous execution, while largely preserving throughput. EE-RL turns this headroom into online savings, reducing GPU energy per valid training token by up to 16.9% at a modest throughput cost.

papers.title: Scheduling Data to Compute: Hierarchical Data Pipelining for LLM Training on AMD GPUs
papers.summary: Large language models (LLM) have been the key focus of recent machine learning breakthroughs. As the model size grows exponentially, the computation needed for training is astronomical. A GPU can do a huge amount of arithmetic. However, the data its compute units need is not always available when they are ready. This data may still be in slow memory or on another GPU. While the chip waits, expensive compute sits idle, and at scale even a small drop in utilization translates into substantial cost. In this paper, we treat this waiting time as the primary bottleneck. We focus on hardware features designed for explicit data movement. These features load data from off-chip memory onto the chip, rearrange it into the layout the computation requires as it is loaded, and transfer it between GPUs. By orchestrating them, we keep a steady pipeline of data flowing to the compute units so that they remain busy. We present kernel and framework implementations that address this bottleneck using three key data-movement instructions and hardware features. The Tensor Data Mover (TDM) moves tensor data from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) into on-chip memory. Transpose-load instructions transpose tensor data into the layout that LLM computations require as it is loaded on-chip. Finally, System DMA (SDMA) and Remote DMA (RDMA) move data between GPUs over the scale-up and scale-out networks, respectively. Our results show that TDM and transpose-load provide on average 1.88x and 1.19x speedup at the kernel level, respectively. The SDMA and RDMA lead to on average 1.16x and 1.33x speedup for computation overlapped with communication. This is the first AMD LLM training system to utilize all the GPU data pipelining features. Our implementation has been integrated into open source framework and library for AMD GPUs. https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus-Turbo https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus

papers.title: Optimization of Joint Beamforming in RIS-aided Multi-carrier and Multi-user MIMO Systems
papers.summary: Reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-aided multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communication is a promising enabler for beyond-fifth-generation wireless networks. However, RIS phase shifters typically rely on a tuning element (for example a variable-length stub), which can be optimally configured for only one carrier frequency at a time. This constraint complicates RIS deployment in multi-carrier systems and often necessitates additional measures, such as using multiple RIS panels or partitioning RIS elements across carriers. In this work, we propose a novel scheme in which all RIS elements simultaneously serve multiple carriers, delivering improved performance over existing approaches. Our method leverages the multiple reflections captured by physically consistent RIS models to realize the desired phase shifts for all carriers using a single stub length setting. We further develop a joint active and passive beamforming optimization framework tailored to multi-carrier, physically consistent RIS-aided systems. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed

papers.title: StarWorld: A Cross-Layer World Model for Starlink Prediction and Streaming
papers.summary: Starlink and other low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite broadband systems exhibit stochastic access dynamics whose effects propagate from network measurements to throughput prediction and adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming, making reasoning over multiple plausible futures essential. Existing studies mainly characterize realized traces or individual system layers, leaving cross-layer world modeling of these evolving dynamics largely unexplored. To address this gap, we propose StarWorld, a cross-layer world model for Starlink prediction and streaming. StarWorld couples learned stochastic network dynamics with executable prediction, control, and playback processes to imagine multi-step cross-layer futures, while a calibrated Trust Gate determines whether these futures are sufficiently reliable for use. On real Starlink measurements, StarWorld achieves the lowest network-future distributional errors among the comparison methods at the principal horizons and reduces pairwise controller quality-of-experience (QoE) effect error by 76%. These results support StarWorld as a cross-layer imagination environment for studying prediction and streaming outcomes under uncertain Starlink access conditions.

papers.title: A Controlled Experimental Evaluation of Configuration and Cache Architecture in LLM Serving Engines
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM applications repeat most of their prompt tokens across requests, and serving engines reuse the cached state of shared prefixes. vLLM and SGLang reuse it at different granularities, and benchmarks of their default deployments report large performance gaps, usually credited to the cache. Such comparisons rarely control for other configuration differences. One of them, whether a long prompt is prefilled in chunks, is set by each engine's defaults from the hardware and the release, and it confounds the comparison. We built a reproducible testbed on Kubernetes and a seeded multi-agent workload generator, and compared the two engines under vendor defaults and with chunked prefill matched. SGLang's configuration is the same in both arms, which makes it an internal control across independently provisioned deployments. Under defaults, vLLM's median time to first token is up to 64x SGLang's. Matching one setting removes 78% of the capacity gap where that gap is largest and 30 to 67% of the latency gap. Near saturation the remaining latency gap reflects queue growth. A fluid queue model driven only by a 4.4% throughput shortfall reproduces it, and shows that such a gap scales with the length of the benchmark run. What survives matching is a tail-latency advantage of 2.4 to 6.4x at equal throughput, consistent with cache-aware ordering of waiting requests. We derive six recommendations for comparing serving engines.

papers.title: Phantom: Temporal Caching for Diffusion Models
papers.summary: Diffusion models have become the dominant paradigm for high-quality image generation, but their iterative inference across tens of timesteps incurs substantial computational overhead. Prior accelerators exploit temporal similarity in diffusion models via differential quantization or output sparsity, yet suffer from increased memory footprint, design complexity, and image degradation. In this work, we present Phantom, an algorithm-architecture co-designed accelerator built on temporal caching. We view temporal similarity as differential sparsity: between adjacent timesteps, only a small fraction of tokens (outliers) change significantly. Phantom recomputes only these outlier tokens and reuses the rest from a temporal cache. Phantom runs on standard systolic arrays with lightweight additions: a Phantom Engine at the global buffer that detects outliers and updates the cache as activations stream through, and a condensed pipeline that maps the resulting sparse updates onto dense systolic computation for FC, convolution, and attention layers. Evaluations on modern diffusion models show that Phantom achieves an average 4.0x speedup and 5.5x energy saving over GPUs and prior accelerators while preserving generation quality.

papers.title: vExpert: Virtualizing Expert Storage for Adaptive Load Balancing in Distributed MoE Inference
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become prevailing, yet their distributed deployment suffers from severe dynamic load imbalance due to the conflict between static expert placement and inherent routing dynamism. While host DRAM offers capacity to avoid static device storage for load balancing, we identify existing offloading works fundamentally fail in distributed inference due to two overlooked challenges: (1) coupled performance impacts of runtime Host-to-Device transfers due to load dynamism and shared PCIe topology; (2) system-level memory overhead incurred by DRAM usage at scale. In this paper, we propose vExpert that shifts DRAM offloading paradigm from partial residency to full redundancy through virtualized expert storage. We pioneer the first systematic performance model that jointly captures H2D latency, PCIe contention, and load imbalance, building a lightweight allocator to dynamically map physical experts to virtual slots runtime. A novel disaggregated manager is designed to reduce memory overhead in multi-process environments. Evaluated on DeepSeek-V3.1 within an 8-node H100 cluster, vExpert improves load balance ratio by up to 55% and achieves 1.2$\times$ end-to-end speedup.

papers.title: File-Semantic SSD for I/O-centric Architectures with NFS-over-NVMe Protocol
papers.summary: Emerging I/O-centric architectures empower peripheral devices to access storage directly while bypassing the host CPU and kernel. However, SSDs expose only a block interface and rely on the host filesystem for file metadata and access control, making file-level access for applications and peripheral devices inherently difficult in I/O-centric architectures. This tight coupling between the host filesystem and storage device introduces unavoidable software overhead and limits the potential of fully hostless I/O paths. In this paper, we present File-Semantic SSD (FS-SSD), a new SSD architecture that provides a native file abstraction within SSDs, enabling direct file access by peripheral and remote devices without host intervention. FS-SSD adopts the lightweight, stateless NFS interface and introduces NFS-over-NVMe, a protocol extension that embeds NFS operations into the standard NVMe command structure. This allows FS-SSD to support local and remote file I/O through existing PCIe and NVMe-oF transports. Our evaluation shows that FS-SSD provides on-device file abstraction while fully utilizing raw-device bandwidth in I/O-centric architectures.

papers.title: TauLang: A Language and Compiler for Space-Time Programming on Statically Scheduled Accelerators
papers.summary: Statically scheduled accelerators such as Groq's Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) achieve low-latency large language model inference by stripping dynamic synchronization hardware from the chip. With no caches, arbiters, or hardware schedulers, the compiler must fix the exact slice and issue cycle of every operation, so when an operation runs is a condition for correctness. Existing kernel languages cannot target such machines because they rely on hardware to resolve cycle timing and instead encode schedules implicitly in code structure. We present TauLang, a kernel language and compiler that makes time a first-class citizen of the program. The programmer schedules operations, loops, and composed kernels with parameterized explicit times, so exploring schedules means changing parameter values rather than rewriting code. TauLang validates explicit times algebraically in TauIR, its timed intermediate representation. It then solves tensor placement and cycle scheduling jointly in an integer linear program, using explicit times to group connected operations into timing clusters that prune the search space. On a cycleaccurate model of a TSP-like machine, joint search achieves a $1.40\times$ latency speedup across ten kernels over a space-first flow. A few explicit time pins keep latency within one cycle of the untimed schedules and scale joint search to 1,636 GEMM blocks, whereas untimed search finds no schedule at 32.

papers.title: Ab Initio Accuracy Beyond the Cutoff: Distributed Message-Passing Equivariant Attention at Tens-of-Millions-of-Atom Scale
papers.summary: Molecular dynamics predicts molecular motion from atomic forces and trajectory integration. Density functional theory (DFT) provides first-principles forces, but its $O(N^3)$ cost limits simulations to thousands of atoms; empirical force fields scale to millions but miss bond breaking and charge transfer. Equivariant message-passing Transformers learn the ab initio potential at linear cost. Stacked layers propagate information beyond a single cutoff, giving four layers a receptive field up to 23{\AA}. At this frontier, scale is limited by communication: layers exchange boundary features across devices, force backpropagation repeats the exchange, and moving atoms change neighbor graphs and tensor shapes. We present Tessera, a distributed runtime that fixes workload shapes between rebuilds. It sorts atoms along a space-filling curve into equal-count shards, ensuring identical atom counts and tensor shapes per rank. Peer sets scale as $K^{0.5}$, not $K$. A conservative neighbor skin preserves topology across updates, enabling each rebuild interval to replay as one CUDA Graph. Fused kernels, three-level neighbor search, and overlapped All-to-All complete it. On 512 GPUs, Tessera sustains 30.7M atoms at 89.7% weak-scaling efficiency (77--90% across three per-GPU loads); per-step time rises 1.11--1.29x as machine and problem grow 16x. Graph reuse cuts full-step time $1.87\times$. Across an $8\times$ device increase, neighbor-search cost grows $1.7\times$, versus $3.0\times$ for Morton order. In a live $10.24$M-atom salt solution, NVE energy drift is $0.42\,\mu$eV/atom/ps over $10$ ps, and structure matches a serial reference. A 10.06M-atom Norovirus capsid sustains 100 ps of NVT at $\approx 8$ ps/day on 256 A100 GPUs. Over 200,000 steps, it has no broken bonds or anomalously close pairs and uses three compiled variants, with no graph breaks or eager fallbacks.

papers.title: CARE-FL: Federated Fine-Tuning of Multimodal LLMs in Resource-Constrained Edge Networks
papers.summary: Domain-specific adaptation of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in privacy-sensitive edge environments requires federated fine-tuning, yet client selection remains challenging due to heterogeneous multimodal data and modality availability, dynamic system conditions, and evolving client utility during training. We propose Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Federated Fine-Tuning (CARE-FL), a constrained online client-selection framework for federated MLLM Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning. CARE-FL formulates client participation as a sequential decision process and employs Q-value decomposition to address the large combinatorial joint action space through scalable client-level long-term utility estimation. These utilities are learned online using a modified Double Deep Q-Learning (DDQL) scheme, while constraint-aware $\epsilon$-greedy execution selects feasible client subsets under per-round latency and bandwidth constraints. Complementing client selection, an adaptive aggregation mechanism further controls potentially unstable global updates and places greater weight on the previous model when needed. Experiments on the CrisisMMD disaster-response task in emulated heterogeneous wireless edge environments show that CARE-FL achieves higher and more stable test accuracy than the compared client-selection baselines across different system settings, while satisfying the imposed latency and bandwidth constraints.

papers.title: Efficient Stable Word-RAM Simulation by Population Protocols
papers.summary: Population protocols model computation by indistinguishable agents interacting in uniformly random pairs, with unary inputs and outputs encoded by state counts. Efficiency requires polylogarithmically many states and polylogarithmic stabilisation time, measured as interactions divided by population size $n$. Stability requires eventual stabilisation to the correct output with probability $1$; silence requires that no agent changes state after stabilisation. Fast stable leader election and majority in leaderless populations require growing state spaces. Despite progress on individual problems, the general computational power of efficient stable protocols remains largely unexplored. We show that it extends beyond semilinear predicates, which characterise constant-state stable computation. We give an efficient, stable, and silent simulation of every $\mathcal{P}$-program: a word-RAM program with running time and number of registers polynomial in $w=\Theta(\log n)$. Stabilisation takes polylogarithmic time both in expectation and with high probability. The framework supports general word-oriented computations, including multiple outputs. The construction extends MC$+$ protocols, fast Monte Carlo protocols whose failures are eventually detected as anomalies, and the system of weights. MC$+$ majority comparisons against the weights convert unary inputs into binary registers, with one agent per bit. MC$+$ operations on individual bits emulate RAM instructions, after which outputs are converted back to unary. A detected anomaly triggers a new universal rank-based backup that stabilises correctly and silently. These results open a systematic study of computational power and resource trade-offs, including extensions to external or spatial data.

papers.title: Chiron: Cache Management Empowered by LLM Intelligence for AI Workloads
papers.summary: AI clusters keep data in remote object stores and rely on local caches to stop GPUs from waiting for data. A cache performs well only when its prefetching and eviction policies match the access pattern, yet these patterns differ across AI workloads and change between phases of one workflow. Existing methods either need code changes, which compromises user transparency, or use low-end heuristics, which cannot follow such changes. Large language models (LLMs) can infer access behavior without user hints, but direct LLM control of cache actions suffers from long reasoning delay, high token cost, and poor decision quality. We present Chiron, a cache system based on advisory switching control. An LLM asynchronously diagnoses the access pattern and recommends a policy. A deterministic harness gates this advice, executes expert-designed policies locally, and returns cache feedback for review. We implement Chiron atop JuiceFS and evaluate it on nine AI workloads. It reduces job completion time by 14.3-41.2% over the best baseline on popular AI workloads.

papers.title: Performance Portability of Out-of-Kernel Optimizations on GPUs: A Molecular Docking Case Study
papers.summary: Achieving performance portability is challenging for irregular scientific applications built as repeated multi-kernel GPU pipelines, because throughput depends on out-of-kernel decisions as much as on kernel efficiency. Using molecular docking as a representative case study, we propose an out-of-kernel tuning methodology that treats batching policy, worker concurrency, and per-worker memory allocation as explicit optimization parameters, replacing backend-dependent occupancy-driven choices with a more portable execution strategy based on explicit resource bounds. We implement this methodology in the muDock mini-app under a manager/worker execution model where multiple host workers share a GPU through independent streams. We then evaluate the methodology on NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs across CUDA, HIP, and SYCL implementations. Across all evaluated platform/backend pairs, the memory-bounded formulation exceeds the peak throughput of the occupancy-guided baseline. The fully tuned methodology improves the end-to-end throughput on all tested configurations, achieving an average speedup of 1.53x over the baseline.

papers.title: Verified Implementation of the Next-gen Borrow Checking Algorithm for Rust via Abstract Interpretation
papers.summary: Borrow checking is a central mechanism for Rust to ensure temporal memory safety. Its correctness is based on the intuition that the Aliasing XOR Mutability discipline guarantees that programs without borrow errors inherently could not access invalid references (i.e., pointers). However, existing work on formalizing borrow checking treats it either as a component of type systems or as symbolic execution describing resource transfer. None provides a direct explanation of the correctness of borrow checking algorithms such as Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL) or Polonius in the official Rust compiler that function more like static pointer analysis. We take a first step toward solving this problem by formalizing Polonius, the next-generation borrow- checking algorithm for the Rust compiler, on a core subset of Rust. We prove its correctness by showing that any program accepted by Polonius does not access invalid references at runtime. The key observation is that, when borrow checking is performed lazily, Polonius could be treated as a forward abstract interpretation on abstract domains recording pointer aliasing (borrowing) relations. By providing a concrete semantics that formally describes the Aliasing XOR Mutability discipline, we prove the soundness of this abstract interpretation, from which we derive memory safety of checked programs. This formulation of Polonius is implemented and formally verified in the abstract interpretation framework of CompCert. The correctness proofs are generated by an agentic AI under human guidance using paper proofs as proof outline. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive formalization and verification of a borrow checking algorithm as manifested in the Rust compiler.

papers.title: Hardwired Distributed Processing Units for Inference: Neural Decisions at the Sensor that Free the Host
papers.summary: We show that a hardwired distributed processing unit (HDPU) can take a neural decision at the sensor and so remove the inference from the host. Built for zebra-crossing detection on a low-cost Artix-7 FPGA, the unit decides on every camera frame in a fixed 2,269,477 clock cycles (34.04 ms depends upon Fpga clk ), inside the 37.49-ms frame period, and on the board it returns the same scores and decisions as its bit-exact software model on all 639 test images. The whole detection path, from camera pixels to decision, takes 1,814 LUTs, with no processor, no operating system and no full-resolution frame store. When the unit answers instead of reporting "not sure", 95.7% of its answers on street photographs are correct, and a hardware contrast stage lifts accuracy on camera-like dashcam frames from 47.7% to 78.2%. The host is spared all of the inference: 8.13 ms of a core in every frame period, where a full-precision ResNet-18 would need more than a frame period even on 16 threads. It also receives 16 bytes per frame instead of 614,400, 38,400 times less. The unit is an 80x60-pixel pipeline feeding a four-layer binarized CNN with 93,408 one-bit weights, verified bit-exactly from a Python model through RTL simulation to the board. Earlier HDPUs did pre-processing (edges, corners, steering); this one shows that the decision itself can move to the sensor.

papers.title: eBPF-Driven Adaptive Lifetime-Aware Data Placement for Shared FDP SSDs
papers.summary: NVMe Flexible Data Placement (FDP) reduces SSD write amplification by separating data with different lifetimes to minimize garbage collection (GC) copying. However, on shared servers, multiple tenants generate more lifetime classes than the available placement handles. Existing approaches rely on static mappings or application-specific knowledge, failing to capture runtime lifetimes and adapt to changing workloads. The challenge is to identify which data die together and determine which classes should be separated to maximize GC savings under a limited handle budget. We present eFDP, an eBPF-based system that automatically learns data lifetimes and manages FDP placement for unmodified applications on a stock Linux kernel. By tracking writes and invalidations, eFDP identifies lifetime classes and estimates the GC copying saved by separating them. It first assigns each tenant a handle, then allocates the remaining handles to the separations offering the greatest savings. It also re-plans placement when active tenants change. With four database tenants on an emulated FDP SSD, eFDP eliminates twice as much excess write amplification as tenant-level isolation and improves every writing tenant's throughput by 19-23%. On an enterprise FDP SSD, given RocksDB's levels, it matches a manually optimized placement using three handles instead of five. After a tenant switch, eFDP re-plans within seven minutes and maintains 25% lower write amplification than the original layout even after an hour.

papers.title: Weaver: Unlocking Blockchain Transaction Parallelism through State-Decoupled Symbolic Execution
papers.summary: Transaction execution remains a major performance bottleneck in blockchains. Existing parallel execution engines are still blocked by slow state accesses on each transaction's critical path, creating a hidden loss of parallelism. This paper presents Weaver, a state-decoupled transaction processing paradigm that enables execution flow to proceed in the absence of concrete state values. Weaver represents states as lightweight symbolic references and records subsequent computation as symbolic expressions while concrete values are fetched on the fly. To handle state-dependent control flow, Weaver predicts the most likely branch direction through hierarchical symbolic pattern matching. Weaver further introduces expression-granular scheduling that evaluates each symbolic expression as soon as its state dependencies are resolved, rather than waiting for the transaction's entire read set, fully exploiting fine-grained intra-transaction parallelism. Evaluation on real Ethereum blocks and synthetic workloads spanning four representative dApps shows that Weaver delivers 41%-63% higher throughput than state-of-the-art parallel execution engines and up to 7.5 times the throughput of serial execution.

papers.title: Optimal Subcubic Byzantine Agreement with Plain PKI
papers.summary: We consider Byzantine Agreement (BA), where $n$ parties run a distributed protocol to agree on a common value, despite $t$ parties being byzantine. In the synchronous setting, a choice must be made between the weaker unauthenticated setting, which only allows $t < n/3$ byzantine parties, and the stronger authenticated setting that allows up to $t < n/2$ byzantine parties. For this latter setting, BA can be solved with optimal resiliency and optimal bit complexity. However, so far, all optimal solutions rely on the use of threshold signatures. This shows a gap compared to regular signatures, where only protocols with cubic complexity are known for optimal resiliency $t < n/2$. We wonder whether this cubic complexity is required without the use of threshold signatures and show that this is not the case. More specifically, given $\kappa$ an upper bound on the size of a hash or signature, we describe a deterministic protocol solving BA with bit complexity $\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{(\sqrt{13} - 1)/2} n^{(\sqrt{13} + 1)/2}) \approx \mathcal{O}(\kappa^{1.303}n^{2.303})$ while having optimal resiliency $t<n/2$ and round complexity $\mathcal{O}(n)$.

papers.title: AtomicFaaS: Offloading Side-Effect Compensation to the Serverless Platform
papers.summary: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) simplifies distributed application development by offloading operational concerns to the platform, but developers remain responsible for recovering from failures. Retries require idempotent functions, which means that developers have to write complex, error-prone code that undoes or skips the already completed operations of a failed function. To address this, we propose AtomicFaaS, a platform extension that provides semantic atomicity for the external side effects of a function invocation, whether the function fails or its instance crashes, without developer-written compensation code. AtomicFaaS intercepts outbound calls and records their effects in a fault-tolerant log, from which the platform compensates leaked effects outside the failed instance. Compared with a manually implemented saga, AtomicFaaS eliminates compensation code and leaves no compensatable effects after any tested failure, while adding ~1 ms per intercepted call. Under load, it lowers the sustainable throughput of CPU-bound functions, while its latency overhead becomes negligible once calls to external services dominate the invocation time.

papers.title: flash-comm: Self-Synchronizing Collective Communication for LLM Decoding
papers.summary: We present flash-comm, a communication library that achieves efficient transport for LLM decoding by fusing readiness synchronization with data movement. flash-comm introduces self-synchronizing transfers in which each data block carries evidence of its readiness, allowing receivers to directly validate the blocks they need without separate inter-GPU barriers. Based on this principle, a cost-guided protocol selector adapts the readiness encoding to message size and the number of participating GPUs, balancing synchronization overhead against additional data-transfer cost. flash-comm further decouples transport order from reduction order to preserve result consistency across GPUs under asynchronous data arrivals. On a server with eight NVIDIA B300 GPUs, flash-comm reduces all-reduce latency by a median of 28.8% and up to 43.7% compared with custom AR v2 (the state-of-the-art all-reduce implementation). In end-to-end decoding, flash-comm reduces time per output token (TPOT) by 1.7-6.8%. Note that all-reduce accounts for 11.4% of the baseline decoding time, which bounds the latency reduction possible from optimizing this operation alone. The same mechanism also supports standalone all-gather, reducing latency by a median of 23.8% and up to 58.9% across eight B300 GPUs.

papers.title: Data Center Agglomeration and Power Infrastructure Capacity in the United States
papers.summary: The continuous expansion of digital infrastructure, especially data centers, has imposed unprecedented, geographically concentrated stress on existing power grids. However, rigorous causal evidence quantifying how these facilities reshape local power-infrastructure supply remains limited. This study builds a comprehensive county-level US panel dataset spanning 2010-2024, uniquely integrating individual data center building footprints and power-plant additions. To mitigate endogeneity and high-dimensional confounding, this study deploys Double Machine Learning with five-fold cross-fitting, conditioning on county and year fixed effects alongside regional socioeconomic covariates. Baseline estimation identifies a significant positive causal effect robust across multiple rigorous specifications. The result holds following 1%-99% winsorization that downweights mega-clusters including Loudoun County: growth in data-center floor area drives meaningful increases in nearby power-generation capacity (ATE=1.982, P=0.000, CI: [1.25, 2.72]). Outcomes remain statistically significant using a one-year lagged treatment to address reverse causality, and are stable under state-level fixed-effect alternatives. An event-study framework augmented with historical agglomeration controls validates clear parallel trends and detects a sharp causal spike at t = 3, matching typical utility-scale grid-construction lead times. A placebo test further verifies these causal estimates cannot emerge from random chance. Substantial regional heterogeneity emerges: strong positive impacts concentrate in the West, while significant negative displacement-related effects appear within resource-constrained Northeastern counties. These results deliver timely insights for urban planners and energy regulators, stressing the importance of forward-looking grid-capacity investment to support ongoing digital transformation.

papers.title: Energy Efficient Near-Threshold Voltage Massive MIMO Computing
papers.summary: Near-Threshold Computing (NTC) offers a substan- tial energy savings, i.e., up to 10x, for digital circuits. However, due to Process, Voltage, and Temperature (PVT) variations, low voltage operating digital processors face increased susceptibility to timing errors. This work equips conventional massive MIMO algorithms with computational error detection mechanisms, en- abling reliable operation down to near-threshold voltages. While conventional hardware based Timing Error Detection (TED) systems introduce substantial overhead, this work modifies MIMO algorithms to seamlessly integrate low overhead Algorithm Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT). A co-simulation framework combining transistor level SPICE simulations and workload aware fault injection is developed to investigate reliability, Bit Error Rate (BER), energy savings, and overheads of modified algorithms operating at low voltages. The transistor-level characterization was performed in PSpice using generic Level-1 Shichman-Hodges CMOS transistor models with Monte Carlo parameter variations. No specific CMOS fabrication process node was assumed. Conse- quently, the reported energy savings are analytical estimates and are not specific to a particular CMOS fabrication technology. We evaluate Gauss Seidel (GS), ADMM based infinity norm detection (ADMIN), and Conjugate Gradient (CG) detectors using circuit derived fault models. Results demonstrate remarkable algorith- mic resilience. Although undetected computational errors in some trials near the Point of First Failure (PoFF) were observed, BER increases by only 0.7% to 1.4%, while beyond PoFF, ABFT reported nearly all erroneous cases. The proposed checksum based ABFT detects most arithmetic and memory errors, with an estimated overhead below 2% for a 64 x 16 MIMO system, decreasing further for larger configurations.

papers.title: Enabling AWS Cloud FPGA Development Using High-Level Vitis HLS
papers.summary: We present a toolchain for development of ML models on AWS EC2 F2 cloud FPGA infrastructure from high-level language, implementing a complete Vitis HLS to HDK bridge to AFI workflow that has been absent from the academic literature despite eight years of AWS FPGA availability. We introduce a four-level methodology (FP32 PyTorch, bit-accurate quantized Python, HLS C-simulation, physical FPGA) to aid in localizing errors, including FPGA-specific circuit errors. Together these tools allow coding agents to effectively implement FPGA designs from user directions, testing and debugging as needed. We document the deployment workflow, timing closure strategies, and practical HLS engineering decisions that proved crucial. We validate using TinyBERT fine-tuned for address Named Entity Recognition, implementing the embedding layer and the first of four encoder layers on the FPGA hardware. Our implementation streams weights from host DRAM, yielding poor performance compared to CPU/GPU implementations; we discuss forward paths.

papers.title: Coexistence-Aware Antenna Tilt and Resource Allocation for Cellular-Connected UAV Corridors
papers.summary: Cellular-connected UAV corridors reuse terrestrial infrastructure to provide predictable aerial connectivity, but coexistence with ground users (GUEs) creates competing demands on antenna tilt and physical resource blocks (PRBs). Prior work optimizes tilt for signal quality alone and does not address joint tilt-PRB planning under corridor rate and GUE delay constraints, nor the allocation policy needed when combined resource claims exceed the PRB budget. We address both gaps by formulating a joint antenna-tilt and PRB-allocation problem that maximizes GUE sum-log-rate subject to a minimum UAV corridor rate and an $ M/G/1$-based GUE mean-delay bound. We decompose the problem into two subproblems: antenna tilts are adapted via projected gradient ascent, while PRB allocation follows a techno-economic approach. Under resource scarcity, we cast the PRB scarcity as a bankruptcy problem and apply the weighted Talmud rule to balance GUE and UAV claims. Simulation results demonstrate that relaxing the GUE delay bound consistently reduces UAV rate dissatisfaction under the proposed allocation.

papers.title: Beyond Crash-to-Patch: Patch Evolution for Linux Kernel Repair
papers.summary: Linux kernel bug repair is typically approached as a direct mapping from crash reports to code patches. In practice, however, kernel fixes undergo iterative revision on mailing lists before acceptance, with reviewer feedback shaping correctness, concurrency handling, and API compliance. This iterative refinement process encodes valuable repair knowledge that existing automated approaches overlook. We present a large-scale study of kernel patch evolution, reconstructing 6946 syzbot-linked bug-fix lifecycles that connect crash reports, reproducers, mailing-list discussions, revision histories, and merged fixes. Our analysis confirms that accepted repairs are frequently non-local and governed by reviewer-enforced constraints not present in bug reports. Building on these insights, we develop PatchAdvisor, a repair framework that integrates retrieval-based memory with a fine-tuned diagnostic advisor to guide a coding agent toward reviewer-aligned patches. Evaluation on temporally held-out syzbot cases demonstrates that leveraging patch-evolution history yields measurable gains in both reviewer-aligned refinement signals and end-to-end repair quality compared to unguided and retrieval-only baselines.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Resource Orchestration for Agentic AI Systems
papers.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems powered by large language models (LLMs) execute as autonomous multi-step pipelines that dynamically invoke tools, integrate observations into memory, and iterate until a task is resolved or a resource budget is exhausted. Unlike classical workflows with fixed graphs, the aggregate compute, bandwidth, and end-to-end latency demands of such pipelines are unknown at dispatch time: they emerge at runtime from intermediate observations and stochastic token sampling, yielding heavy-tailed, multi-modal random variables. This unpredictability forces infrastructure orchestrators into a dilemma: under-provisioning risks mid-execution throttling and deadline violations, while over-provisioning wastes scarce edge or cloud capacity. Existing schedulers require a fully known pipeline graph, while edge resource-management methods rely on parametric or stationary demand models, and neither fits the unknown, non-stationary profiles of agentic pipelines. We formalize this setting as the uncertainty-aware agentic orchestration problem, where the goal is to reserve, at dispatch time, compute and bandwidth allocations that cover actual pipeline demands, and to verify that the pipeline can meet its deadline, each with a prescribed probability. We then propose Conformal Reservation for Orchestration (CRO), an online algorithm that translates a sliding window of past execution traces into dispatch-time resource allocations with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees via conformal prediction. Simulations over heterogeneous task mixes with multi-modal and heavy-tailed profiles show that CRO is the only evaluated method that simultaneously satisfies target probabilistic coverage across all risk levels while, among coverage-feasible methods, attaining the lowest over-reservation, roughly halving the resource waste of the Chebyshev-bound baseline.

papers.title: A Feasibility Condition for Confidence-Gated Tiered LLM Inference
papers.summary: Tiered inference distributes large language model computation across a hierarchy of devices, from on-device and edge hardware to the datacenter, and is increasingly offered as the route to cheaper, lower-latency, and more private serving. Most such systems orchestrate frozen model checkpoints, and most decide what to resolve locally and what to escalate using a confidence signal produced by a forward-deployed model. We give a closed-form condition for when no threshold on that signal makes a tiered cascade worthwhile relative to sending every query to the backstop. Modeling the routing decision as a binary test and separating local from escalation cost through an architecture cost ratio $\kappa$, we derive a feasibility condition bracketed by a signal-free floor, below which a cascade is feasible at any signal quality, and a perfect-signal ceiling, above which none is. Read along the $\kappa$ axis the condition inverts: where local compute is billed, cost binds, matching a recent empirical finding; where it is sunk, on decentralized hardware, feasibility becomes unconditional and signal quality instead sets what the cascade achieves. We turn the condition into three design requirements that existing trained-in primitives satisfy only in isolation, and we propose, as future work, a co-designed architecture and a protocol to test it. The condition and the inversion hold independently of that architecture; they are the paper's contribution.

papers.title: Easy Multi-Precision Acceleration via Vectorization
papers.summary: High level programming languages and accelerators are powerful enablers for a wide range of applications. Accelerators offer significant performance via diverse numeric precision and increased memory bandwidth and capacity. These enable new algorithms to be explored. Construction of these algorithms can be enabled by the ready accessibility of these performance features in high-level languages. Achieving scalable vertical (within a compute node), precision (over various numeric precisions), and temporal (over different generations of hardware) performance while retaining productivity requires effective abstractions. Vectorized coding that expresses operations as high-level matrix mathematics has historically been an important method for achieving portable performance. This paper examines the performance availability across a wide range of precisions and hardware using simple vectorized coding techniques applied to several example programs that highlight bandwidth, real and complex matrix multiplication, and 2D convolution. The systems evaluated span nearly a decade of computing hardware, enabling direct comparison of performance gains over this period. This work demonstrates that near hardware peak performance is readily accessible from high-level programming environments. In particular for memory bandwidth, real and complex matrix multiplication in double/single/half precision, and 2D convolutions using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). Furthermore, algorithms that trade decreased compute intensity for increased memory intensity have significant potential.

papers.title: RESHPart: Feedback-Reshaped Spectral Embedding for Hypergraph Partitioning
papers.summary: With scalable Laplacian solvers now available, the next frontier is to exploit them more effectively for high-quality hypergraph partitioning. In this work, we revisit spectral hypergraph partitioning from the perspective of spectral embedding geometry. Through a systematic analysis of circuit hypergraphs and controlled synthetic (hyper)graphs, we identify a ray-like embedding structure that helps explain the effectiveness of projection-based partitioning. We further show that the geometry of spectral embeddings can be systematically influenced through Laplacian design and hyperedge reweighting. Guided by these insights, we propose FRESHPart, a feedback-reshaped spectral partitioning framework that refines the spectral embedding through Geometry Feedback and Search Feedback, producing embeddings that are better aligned with projection-based partitioning. On the Titan23 benchmark, FRESHPart achieves average cut reductions over hMETIS of 13.09% at $\epsilon=2\%$ and 25.21% at $\epsilon=20\%$, surpassing the strongest previously reported results (12.16% and 22.53%, respectively), while completing every benchmark in under 120 s on a single GPU.

papers.title: CHARM+: Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism
papers.summary: As sequence lengths continue to grow, distributed attention based on sequence parallel (e.g., Ring-Attention) has become a mainstream solution for large language models (LLMs). Nevertheless, inherent communication dependencies limit computation-communication overlap, reducing GPU utilization. Moreover, in cross-hardware (NUMA or node) architectures, due to imbalanced communication bandwidth, frequent communication synchronization will limit overall performance. Based on these insights, we propose CHARM+, Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism. We reorganize sequential communications into several levels and achieve intra-level parallelism and computation overlap. Furthermore, we decouple cross-hardware communication from intra-hardware communication, eliminating synchronization overhead caused by bandwidth imbalance. Forward and backward algorithms were evaluated on multiple hardware architectures and consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods. Compared to Ring-Attention, our forward and backward algorithms achieve average speedups of 1.3x and 1.7x on a dual-NUMA PCIe architecture, and 2.8x and 2.9x on a dual-node NVLink architecture, respectively.

papers.title: Ray-Tracing-Based Dynamic Channel Sounding With Autoregressive Wi-Fi CSI Prediction
papers.summary: Channel sounding in Wi-Fi multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems must balance channel state information (CSI) accuracy against CSI acquisition overhead. Device mobility causes channel aging, while autoregressive CSI prediction introduces errors that accumulate over sounding intervals. However, standardized statistical channel models cannot fully capture the environment-specific channel dynamics encountered in physical artificial intelligence (AI) applications, motivating the use of Sionna-based ray tracing to evaluate CSI prediction under device mobility and evolving propagation geometry. This paper develops a dynamic sounding framework that integrates autoregressive CSI prediction with signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR)-constrained interval selection. A Transformer with rotary position embedding that converts device positions into CSI sequences predicts CSI across multiple subcarriers for beamforming updates between sounding exchanges. We formulate sounding-interval selection as a predicted average-throughput maximization problem under per-stream SINR lower-bound constraints, including CSI acquisition and processing overhead. A prediction-error perturbation analysis provides the SINR bounds, and cumulative-sum enumeration globally solves the finite single-variable problem. Actual SINR feasibility holds whenever the prediction errors satisfy the bounds. Ray-tracing experiments assess channel prediction, trajectory transfer, and autoregressive prediction errors. In single-STA Wi-Fi 7 link-level simulations, predicted-CSI beamforming improves mean goodput by 67.3%, 112.7%, and 119.1% over stale CSI for linear, circular, and cosine trajectories, respectively.

papers.title: Enforcing Accountable Disclosure in Confidential AI
papers.summary: Advances in CPU and GPU confidential computing enable confidential AI, allowing LLMs to process user prompts without exposing them to service providers or infrastructure operators. However, AI agents often need to send prompt-derived information to external services, and providers may also require limited disclosure for safety monitoring and failure diagnosis. We propose CORDE, a system for confidential virtual machines (CVMs) designed to satisfy the principle of Confine or Declare: user-derived data is confined by default, but when necessary, it may leave the CVM only after being "declared." To "declare" data is to record its exact contents, recipient, and stated reason in a user-accessible, tamper-evident declaration log. To put this principle into practice, we present an integrated system design that combines per-user information-flow control in Rust with a TEE-based ledger and remote attestation. Our evaluation on an NVIDIA H100 GPU shows that declaration before disclosure adds little overhead in task latency, about 0.5% on the AppWorld agent benchmark. CORDE provides a basis for accountable disclosure of user data, supporting responsible and transparent data management in AI services.

papers.title: CoordX Protocol: Peer to Peer Cryptographically Verified Shared Records
papers.summary: People, companies and software agents often must work on shared records even when they do not trust each other. Today they usually give those records to a central server. The server keeps the canonical copy, authenticates users, and decides who has permissions to act on the record. The CoordX Protocol removes the need for that central server. In the CoordX protocol the author of a record holds full permission over it. Permission for any other party to create, read or update the record is assigned by explicit grants and keys. An invitation only starts contact between two parties. It gives no permission. Each record is a causal tree of signed entries, and each entry is immutable. Each entry names the permission that allowed it. Any party can get the proof of that permission and check it without help from anyone. Two honest parties that check the same bytes, with the same keys and local settings, always get the same answer. The content is encrypted, so the relays that may carry it in transit see only sealed bytes. To exclude a party from future content, the other parties move to new keys. The protocol does not choose a winning version, does not put entries in time order, and does not need global agreement. Applications decide what the entries mean above the level of the protocol.

papers.title: PIMROP: A Feasibility Study of Return-Oriented Programming on Commercial Processing-in-Memory Architectures
papers.summary: Processing-in-Memory places small programmable cores on the memory device, where they execute beside the DRAM banks and beyond the control-flow defenses that protect host programs. The security of this in-memory code is an attack surface that remains largely unstudied. We present PIMROP, to our knowledge the first demonstrated code-reuse attack on a commercial Processing in-Memory ISA. We show that return-oriented programming is feasible on a real, commercially shipped PIM instruction set, the UPMEM DPU, whose DRAM Processing Units run C compiled by a dedicated LLVM toolchain. We build Galileo-for-DPU, a gadget scanner adapted to the DPU's fixed-width, 8-byte-aligned RISC encoding, and run it entirely on the UPMEM functional simulator in a reproducible Docker and VM environment. We find the runtime library that every kernel links already yields 517 non-trivial gadgets covering all five canonical ROP primitive classes, and all 13 PrIM benchmarks we scanned carry gadgets as well. We then demonstrate two verified end-to-end attacks, each reproducible on 10 of 10 runs. In the first, a stack buffer overflow in a DPU kernel overwrites the saved return address and diverts control into a routine that copies a secret into host-readable memory. In the second, we leak the same secret using a chain of reused gadgets alone, without diverting control into any such routine. We further show that two standard defenses--stack canaries and _FORTIFY_SOURCE-style bounds-check fortification--fail on the DPU in ways specific to the platform (misplaced canary, silently inactive wrapper), and we verify a bounds-checked DMA that stops the attack on 10 of 10 runs with no effect on benign requests. To enable further research on PIM security, we open-source Galileo-for-DPU and our testing harness at https://github.com/wtegge2/ROP-in-PIM.

papers.title: Shallow Encoding Emits Deep Memories
papers.summary: Hybrid language models interleave a few softmax-attention layers with many linear-attention or state-space layers, so every layer keeps a memory of earlier tokens: a key-value cache or a fixed-size recurrent state. Serving them spends more compute and high-bandwidth memory on these memories than the output requires. The prefill runs every layer for every prompt token, and every decode step loads and stores whole recurrent states, which on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next take as many bytes per request as the attention cache of thousands of tokens. We find two properties of trained hybrids that locate this excess. First, writes are easier than reads: writing a deep layer's memory of a token needs little of the deep computation that predicting the next token needs. Trained copies of the deep layers' write paths, which we call emitters, therefore write a prompt's deep memories from the residual stream of a shallower anchor layer, and all prompt tokens but the last run as few as 63% of the layers. Second, recurrent states have a state sink: most of their energy lies in a rank-one term along a fixed direction of each head, and the rest is a low-rank working memory. SEED builds on both: it makes the prefill shallow in depth and the decode state shallow in representation. Each recurrent state is stored as its sink plus low-rank factors, which the Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention and Mamba-2 updates extend exactly; we prove that the open-loop error of the periodic compressions back to low rank is bounded independently of their number. SEED keeps the original weights frozen, compresses no attention cache, and runs all layers for every generated token. On six checkpoints of five production hybrids of 30B to over 300B parameters, it is nearly lossless on eleven official exams. Served with SGLang on NVIDIA GB300 GPUs on an agentic-coding trace, it raises the per-GPU throughput of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 1.2-1.4x.

papers.title: Constant-Round Massively Parallel Algorithms for Approximate MSTs in Metric Spaces
papers.summary: We develop a unified algorithmic framework for computing approximate minimum spanning trees (MSTs) in metric spaces in the fully scalable Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model. Using this framework, we obtain the following results for any fixed constant $\sigma\in(0,1)$: - General metrics: Given all pairwise distances, we compute a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate MST in $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ rounds using $n^\sigma$ local space per machine and $\widetilde{O}(n^2)$ total space. - Euclidean spaces: Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we compute an $O(1/\sigma^4)$-approximate MST in $O(1)$ rounds using $(nd)^\sigma$ local space per machine and $O(nd+n^{1+\sigma})$ total space. - Doubling metrics: Given $n$ points in a metric of doubling dimension $\mathrm{ddim}=O(\sigma\log n)$, we compute an $O(1/\sigma)$-approximate MST in $O(\mathrm{ddim}/\sigma^4)$ rounds using $n^\sigma$ local space per machine and $\widetilde{O}(n^{1+\sigma})\cdot 2^{O(\mathrm{ddim})}$ total space. For any fixed constant $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, these results give the first constant-round MPC algorithms achieving $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation in general metrics and $O(1)$-approximation in a high-dimensional Euclidean space, respectively. They improve upon the $O(\log\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon))$-round algorithm for general metrics [SODA'25] and the $O(\log\log n\cdot\log\log\log n)$-round algorithm for Euclidean spaces [SODA'24], respectively. Moreover, our round complexity for general metrics is asymptotically optimal in its dependence on $\varepsilon$, matching the $\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ lower bound of [SODA'25] under the 1-vs-2-cycles conjecture. Our result also answers an open question raised by [STOC'23].

papers.title: Mobility-Aware Mobile Edge Computing for Energy-Balanced Data Collection in IoT-Enabled Underwater Sensor Networks
papers.summary: Underwater wireless sensor networks (UWSNs) face critical challenges in energy imbalance, connectivity, and data collection due to harsh environments. To address these issues, this paper focuses on the problem is how to achieve energy-balanced data collection in IoT-enabled UWSNs with a mobility-aware mobile edge computing (MEC), named MECEBDC. Unlike existing approaches, the proposed scheme jointly optimizes energy-aware clustering, cluster head selection, and AUV-assisted data collection. Furthermore, we design a novel metaheuristic-based AUV routing algorithm that incorporates realistic underwater mobility dynamics, explicitly considering gravitational pressure and buoyancy forces acting on the AUV. By leveraging the computing, storage, and mobility capabilities of MEC-enabled AUVs, the proposed approach enables efficient trajectory planning and adaptive data gathering in a stable 3D underwater environment. Extensive simulations and theoretical analysis demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces node energy consumption, improves data collection efficiency, and prolongs network lifetime compared with existing schemes, making it well suited for long-term underwater IoT applications.

papers.title: Explainable Anomaly Detection in 5G Networks through Continuous Time Graphs
papers.summary: 5G networks increasingly resemble distributed systems in their design. It then becomes crucial to move beyond traditional network-based detection methods and to explore alternative approaches. In this work, we propose a formalization of 5G network exchanges as a dynamic graph, on which we apply techniques from the field of graph-based learning to detect anomalies effectively. This representation allows for fine-grained analysis of packet-level semantic content, while simultaneously capturing sequential and topological contexts, both of which are essential for identifying sophisticated and multi-stage attacks. To assess the effectiveness of this formalism, we evaluate it with the most popular dynamic graph models, demonstrating its potential for 5G anomaly detection.

papers.title: Clear Human Web: Where a Person Vouches for Every Client
papers.summary: The web cannot tell whether a request comes from a person or from a program. Sites have checked the network address and puzzles in its place, and both have given way: automated traffic exceeds human traffic, and puzzles are solved for pay and by agents. This paper proposes the Clear Human Web, the part of the public web that sites open only to clients a person vouches for. A person's wallet presents their person identification data (PID) to one issuer, the only party that registers as a relying party, and receives a bounded number of blind-signed tokens, proofs of personhood that carry no attribute. The browser spends one token at each site that runs the gate, and the site learns that a valid token of a trusted issuer was spent, and nothing else. No field is added to the PID, no protocol is introduced, no site registers, and the publisher of a site holds the same proof as its readers. We define the Clear Human Web through five properties and seven adversaries, and state which properties the construction satisfies against each adversary. The identities a person can hold on one site in an epoch are bounded to k. The bound holds once the wallet limits a person to one pseudonym at the issuer. In the optimum k = 1, and a zero-knowledge proof of PID possession and a pseudonym per site replace the tokens.

papers.title: Spatial Path Superposition: A No-Cloning Perspective on MIMO-Inspired Spatial Diversity
papers.summary: Spatial diversity is a key mechanism in classical Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) communications, where multiple propagation alternatives provide redundant observations that improve reliability in noisy environments. A direct translation of this principle to quantum communications is forbidden by the no-cloning theorem, since an unknown quantum state cannot be copied and transmitted through independent links. In this Perspective article, we argue that spatial path superposition provides a no-cloning-compatible analogue of the spatial-diversity principle of MIMO. Rather than duplicating the transmitted quantum state, a quantum carrier is coherently delocalized over multiple communication links, so that alternative spatial evolutions are experienced in quantum superposition. In this framework, classical redundancy is replaced by spatial coherence, and the communication link itself becomes part of the quantum dynamics. Indeed, spatial coherence can enhance the fidelity of the received quantum state, providing the quantum counterpart of the classical diversity gain, and can be converted into bipartite and multipartite entanglement during propagation. This implies that, under suitable coherent path control, noisy channel evolutions can contribute constructively to entanglement generation. This Perspective identifies spatial path superposition as a quantum-native primitive for the Quantum Internet, linking no-cloning-compatible spatial diversity, fidelity enhancement, entanglement generation, and coherent path control.

papers.title: When Does Risk-Controlled Throughput Forecasting Actually Control Risk? A Reproduction Study on LEO Satellite Link
papers.summary: Risk-budgeted throughput forecasting converts a point forecast of LEO satellite capacity into a conservative bound whose overestimation rate is held at a user-specified budget, so that admission control can act on it safely. We reproduce the state of the art, BG-CFQS, on the three Starlink traces its authors used and on an independent fourth dataset, and report four findings. First, its risk guarantee is reproducible but conditional on the calibration split: under a random split we recover every published quantity, including risk-pass on 3 of 3 datasets, but under a contiguous temporal split, which is what a deployed terminal faces, it holds on 1 of 3. Second, independent of any split, the method cannot serve a risk budget below 0.15, the low end of its candidate quantile set. On all four datasets the achieved rate is identical at budgets of 0.05, 0.10 and 0.15, overshooting by 1.4x to 3.7x at the tightest. Third, static conformal calibration cannot improve a ranking, only shift an operating point; we confirm this exactly on latency spike detection, where online calibration improves AUPRC by up to 51%. Fourth, group-conditional online recalibration splits into two mechanisms. The online part replicates: it tracks the budget within 1% from 0.05 to 0.35, where static calibration is 16 to 21% off. The group-conditional part does not: on three of four datasets, conditioning on any available covariate, including measured serving-satellite geometry, is worse than not conditioning, and our attempt to predict which datasets benefit failed. What is new here is empirical, not algorithmic: we claim the findings, not the methods.

papers.title: Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts
papers.summary: AI's inflection point is a fountain of alarming risks. Digital platforms in particular are vulnerable to three major AI risks, as those in control of global platforms cede control to AI, of the algorithms, of membership and of content: (1) AI control of global platforms, social and economic, used by the majority of humanity, resulting in the majority of humanity becoming vulnerable to AI control. (2) Unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously on social and economic digital platforms, side-by-side with humans, possibly masquerading as humans, serving unknown masters with unknown goals, operating under unknown restraints without accountability or culpability. (3) Unattributed deepfakes generated by anonymous AI, with people unable to distinguish them from genuine content and with their producers evading accountability and culpability. Here, we propose to corral these AI risks with grassroots contracts, a digital incarnation of a two-centuries old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. We present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and working smartphone apps that implement the two and show how they corral these major AI risks: (1) AI control of global platforms. (2) Unaccountable AI agents. (3) Unattributed deepfakes.

papers.title: FPTR: Feasibility-Preserving Transactional Refinement for Deadline-Constrained Joint Beam and Resource Allocation
papers.summary: Short-interval wireless schedulers must return a complete, feasible beam-and-resource allocation before each execution deadline, and a late or invalid output gives no utility in the current control cycle. Searching longer can increase transmitted traffic, but it may also miss the deadline or leave only an infeasible intermediate solution. We propose Feasibility-Preserving Transactional Refinement (FPTR), which always keeps a validated feasible allocation, the incumbent. Each refinement stage builds a separate candidate and leaves the incumbent unchanged. A candidate replaces the incumbent only if it is complete, passes the feasibility validator before its stage cutoff, and strictly improves the objective; otherwise it is discarded. Four refinement stages use this rule: buffer-aware resource selection, compatibility-group (CG) user sharing, beam-mask rebuilding from remaining demand, and joint reassignment of two resources. On 150 fixed synthetic instances, the full pipeline (Full) raises traffic by 3.83% on average over a lightweight beam-first reference and by 1.79% over its Base constructor. In a separate suite with matched inputs, Full exceeds six independent search baselines (ALNS, tabu search, GA, simulated annealing, iterated local search, and GRASP) by 6.68-8.35%, where outputs later than 100 ms receive zero utility. All 750 Full runs in the internal suite returned feasible allocations, and none exceeded 100 ms. Separating mandatory output construction from optional refinement lets spare computation time improve the allocation without endangering the incumbent. The open-source implementation supports independent reproduction.

papers.title: Distributed Consensus, Optimization, and Learning under Communication Constraints
papers.summary: Many modern engineering applications require distributed problem-solving in which multiple nodes in a network cooperate to achieve a common optimization objective. Numerous distributed optimization and learning algorithms rely on consensus-based distributed coordination to ensure network-wide agreement via iterative local interactions. In these algorithms, the accuracy, frequency, and reliability of information exchange among network nodes directly influence system performance, including convergence behavior, training delay, and model accuracy. This tutorial article adopts a bottom-up approach to present the fundamentals of consensus averaging and distributed optimization methods, and highlights the impact of network connectivity, information flow, and communication uncertainty on network cooperation and optimization performance. Building on these theoretical insights, we discuss key design principles for communication-constrained distributed learning across diverse network topologies and review common approaches to communication-efficient learning, particularly in wireless networks. Despite substantial progress, further efforts are needed to bridge the gap between theory and practice and fully realize the potential of cooperative and networked intelligence.

papers.title: RCOMPSs: A Scalable Runtime System for R Code Execution on Manycore Systems
papers.summary: R has become a cornerstone of scientific and statistical computing due to its extensive package ecosystem, expressive syntax, and strong support for reproducible analysis. However, as data sizes and computational demands grow, native R parallelism support remains limited. This paper presents RCOMPSs, a scalable runtime system that enables efficient parallel execution of R applications on multicore and manycore systems. RCOMPSs adopts a dynamic, task-based programming model, allowing users to write code in a sequential style, while the runtime automatically handles asynchronous task execution, dependency tracking, and scheduling across available resources. We present RCOMPSs using three representative data analysis algorithms, i.e., K-nearest neighbors (KNN) classification, K-means clustering, and linear regression and evaluate their performance on two modern HPC systems: KAUST Shaheen-III and Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC) MareNostrum 5. Experimental results reveal that RCOMPSs demonstrates both strong and weak scalability on up to 128 cores per node and across 32 nodes.
